strengths: Novel and timely combination of the martingale posterior (MGP) framework with a foundation tabular model (TabPFN), addressing a genuine practical need: recovering epistemic uncertainty for a user-defined scientific estimand from a pretrained predictor without requiring likelihood-prior elicitation.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 30 setups (11 synthetic, 19 real datasets) spanning linear regression, binary logistic regression, and multinomial logistic regression, with systematic comparison against four competing constructions (Bayesian bootstrap, copula-based MGP, classical Bayes, asymptotic approximation).

The paper is unusually candid about the theoretical gap: it explicitly tests whether TabPFN's predictive rule satisfies the martingale or the weaker a.c.i.d. condition, finds it does not, and still argues (with supporting diagnostics) that useful epistemic uncertainty can be obtained—this honest treatment of limitations is a strength rather than a weakness.

Diagnostic toolkit (path-stability/L1 convergence, frequentist coverage, posterior contraction) offers a practical way to sanity-check MGP validity for black-box predictive rules where formal verification is currently intractable, which could be useful more broadly.
Reasonably thorough documentation of experimental settings, loss function specification, identifiability constraints, and dataset details in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
Correctly situates the work relative to closely related concurrent efforts (Nagler & Rügamer, Fortini et al.) and clarifies the distinction in approach.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification for validity is essentially absent: the paper shows TabPFN's predictive rule violates both the martingale property and the more general a.c.i.d. condition, and substitutes theory with empirical diagnostics whose sufficiency for validity is asserted rather than established; the diagnostics (L1 path stability, coverage, contraction) are ad hoc sanity checks rather than a new theoretical contribution.

Coverage results are inconsistent: in the synthetic logistic-regression setups (Table 2) and several real-data marginal intervals (e.g., blood, GMM link settings), TabMGP undercovers relative to the 0.95 nominal target, undermining the claim of 'near-nominal coverage' as a general property.

The real-data 'ground truth' θ(F⋆) is defined as the risk minimizer on the entire available dataset, which is a finite-sample proxy rather than a true population quantity; this could bias coverage assessments in ways not discussed.

TabMGP is markedly more computationally expensive (70–200s per posterior sample vs. <20s for all baselines), which combined with TabPFN's context-length limit (~10k) constrains applicability to larger n or higher-dimensional θ (as acknowledged for the regression concentration experiment).

The argument for why generic in-context-learning transformers (e.g., LLMs) are unsuitable as predictive rules while TabPFN is suitable is largely qualitative (permutation invariance, approximate Bayesian training) without direct empirical comparison to any non-TabPFN transformer baseline.

The Copula baseline's bandwidth is fixed manually (0.8) after noting the built-in tuning procedure performs poorly, which may bias comparisons against the copula method and raises questions about whether the reported deficiencies of Copula are inherent or an artifact of suboptimal hyperparameter choice.
Diagonal covariance approximation used for constructing MGP credible ellipsoids (Appendix E.4) is a simplification whose impact on reported 'size' comparisons across methods is not analyzed.

strengths: Novel and timely combination of the martingale posterior (MGP) framework with TabPFN, a state-of-the-art tabular foundation model, avoiding the hand-crafted predictive rules (copula-based updates, Newton's algorithm) and associated hyperparameter tuning that have limited prior MGP constructions.

Extensive and carefully designed empirical evaluation spanning 30 setups (11 synthetic, 19 real-world datasets) across linear regression, binary logistic regression, and multinomial logistic regression, with comparisons to Bayesian bootstrap, copula-based MGP, asymptotic Gaussian approximation, and standard Bayesian posteriors, plus substantial supplementary experiments (semi-synthetic MLP setups, diffuse-prior Bayes, TabPFN-initialised copula) that strengthen robustness of the conclusions.

Intellectually honest treatment of theoretical limitations: the authors explicitly test whether TabPFN's predictive rule satisfies the martingale or the weaker a.c.i.d. sufficient conditions, find that it does not strictly do so, and instead propose and apply practical empirical diagnostics (path stability, frequentist coverage, posterior contraction) to assess validity — a useful contribution for practitioners applying MGP with black-box predictive rules.

Good positioning within the post-Bayesian/BPI/generalised-Bayes literature, with a thorough related-work review of predictive-rule constructions and clear articulation of why TabPFN's permutation invariance and PPD-approximating training make it a natural fit compared to generic transformers.
High reproducibility: detailed algorithm pseudocode, explicit hyperparameters, checkpoint versions, dataset sources, and loss-function specifications are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: No theoretical guarantee is established for the existence of the limiting measure F∞ when using TabPFN as the predictive rule; the paper relies entirely on empirical diagnostics (visual/quantitative L1 convergence, coverage) rather than any formal relaxed sufficient condition, which limits the rigor of the central claim that TabMGP produces valid posteriors in general.

The feature (X) forward-sampling relies on a separate, somewhat ad hoc mechanism (Bayesian bootstrap) decoupled from TabPFN's own capabilities, creating an inconsistency between how X and Y|X are modeled within the same rollout.

Experiments are restricted to fairly small sample sizes (n as low as 20–200) and simple loss functions (linear/logistic/multinomial regression); TabPFN's context-length limitation (10,000) is acknowledged as a practical constraint that was not fully explored, raising questions about scalability to larger or more complex problems.

Per-sample computation cost of TabMGP (70–200s) is substantially higher than competing baselines, and while parallelizability is noted, no wall-clock scalability analysis is provided for larger N or more rollouts.

The evaluation lacks comparison to other modern uncertainty quantification approaches outside the MGP/Bayesian family (e.g., conformal prediction, deep ensembles), which would help contextualize the practical value of TabMGP relative to broader UQ toolkits.

The credible-set 'size' metric uses a diagonal covariance approximation for martingale posteriors (due to limited posterior samples), which could bias size comparisons against methods with fuller covariance estimates and makes some coverage/size comparisons less directly interpretable.
The Impact Statement is minimal and does not meaningfully engage with any potential downstream risks of deploying opaque foundation-model-based posteriors in scientific inference.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: how to obtain calibrated epistemic uncertainty for a scientific estimand θ when practitioners rely on a black-box foundation model (TabPFN) rather than a bespoke likelihood-prior pair.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: 11 synthetic and 19 real-data setups, covering linear regression, binary logistic regression, and multinomial logistic regression, with 100 repetitions per setup and comparisons against four competing posterior constructions (BB, Copula, Bayes, Asymptotic).

The authors are commendably transparent about the method's limitations, explicitly showing in Appendix C that TabPFN's predictive rule does not satisfy the martingale property nor the weaker a.c.i.d. condition, and they discuss concrete failure modes (undercoverage in small n/p classification settings, slow convergence in some setups) in the conclusion.

A substantial battery of diagnostics is provided (path-stability/L1 convergence, sensitivity to rollout length, semi-synthetic checks, alternative posterior constructions, marginal interval coverage across ~293 parameters), which aids reproducibility and gives readers tools to assess when the method may be trusted.
The related-work section is thorough and situates the contribution well relative to existing martingale posterior constructions and concurrent work (e.g., Nagler & Rügamer).
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification is weak: the paper's own diagnostics (Appendix C) show TabPFN's predictive rule departs from both the martingale property and the more general a.c.i.d. condition, i.e., the only formal sufficient conditions the field currently has for the existence of F∞. The paper's response is to substitute purely empirical diagnostics (L1 path stability) for a rigorous existence argument, which is a considerable evidentiary gap for a method whose entire output (a 'martingale posterior') is only meaningful if F∞ exists; a plateauing scaled-L1 trajectory does not by itself certify convergence to a well-defined limiting law and could reflect other saturation effects (e.g., bounded parameter ranges, TabPFN's binning/discretization).

Many reported coverage rates for TabMGP are near or at 1.00 in the synthetic setups (Table 1), which — together with credible-set sizes that are often comparable to or larger than Copula's — suggests the method may frequently be conservative rather than genuinely 'sharp,' undercutting the abstract's claim that TabMGP 'often outperforms' alternatives on both coverage and size simultaneously.

Baseline comparisons may be partly strawman: 'Asymptotic' and 'Bayes' with Hessian-based Gaussian priors are known a priori to perform poorly in the small-n regime the paper specifically selects, so outperforming them is a comparatively low bar and does not by itself establish TabMGP's competitiveness against a well-tuned classical Bayesian analysis.

There is a methodological asymmetry in the construction of joint credible sets: TabMGP, BB, and Copula use a diagonal covariance approximation (Appendix E.4, justified by limited posterior samples), while Bayes and Asymptotic use full covariance matrices. This inconsistency could differentially bias coverage/size comparisons depending on the true parameter correlation structure, and is not explored via sensitivity analysis.

The Copula bandwidth is manually fixed at 0.8 because the method's own default marginal-likelihood tuning 'produces values that are too small and delivers poor results' (Appendix E.1); overriding a competing method's native hyperparameter-selection procedure with a hand-picked value risks under- or over-stating its performance relative to TabMGP, which needs no comparable tuning.

TabMGP is computationally far more expensive than all baselines (70–200s per sample vs. near-instantaneous or 10–20s for competitors), and this gap is only partially explained (uncompiled PyTorch vs. compiled JAX) without any attempt to quantify what a compiled implementation would cost; this materially limits practical applicability, especially given the need for L=100 independent rollouts per credible set.

The definition of ground truth in real-data setups (θ of the empirical distribution over the full dataset) combined with repeated non-i.i.d. train/test splits from the same finite population introduces potential dependence across the 100 repetitions used to compute coverage, which is not discussed as a possible source of bias in the reported frequentist coverage rates.

The theoretical contribution is fairly modest: the paper largely repackages an existing framework (MGP) with an existing predictive engine (TabPFN) plus a Bayesian-bootstrap treatment of covariates (already used by Fong et al., 2023); the primary novelty is empirical rather than methodological or theoretical, which somewhat limits the paper's originality claims.

strengths: Novel and timely synthesis: the paper connects the martingale posterior (MGP)/Bayesian predictive inference framework with a state-of-the-art tabular foundation model (TabPFN), motivated by TabPFN's built-in row-permutation invariance and its training objective that approximates a Bayesian PPD -- properties that make it a natural, well-justified fit for the predictive-rule role in MGP construction.

Extensive and carefully designed empirical evaluation: 30 setups (11 synthetic, 19 real-world datasets) spanning linear regression, binary logistic regression, and multinomial logistic regression, with 100 repetitions per setup and comparisons against five competing posterior constructions (BB, Copula, Bayes, Asymptotic, plus additional diffuse-prior and TabPFN-initialized-copula baselines in the appendix).

Honest and rigorous treatment of theoretical limitations: rather than overclaiming, the authors explicitly test whether TabPFN satisfies the martingale/a.c.i.d. sufficient conditions (Appendix C), find that it does not strictly satisfy them, and are transparent that formal existence of F_infinity cannot currently be proven for high-capacity transformers -- while still providing a principled empirical justification (path stability, coverage, contraction diagnostics) for treating the resulting posterior as useful.

Practical diagnostic toolkit (scaled L1 path-stability, frequentist coverage checks, posterior contraction) that gives practitioners actionable guidance for assessing when TabMGP outputs should be trusted, which is valuable given the lack of formal guarantees.

High reproducibility: detailed appendices specify exact TabPFN checkpoints, hyperparameters, loss function identifiability constraints, dataset construction/stratification procedures, and credible-set construction methods.
The method requires no hand-tuned smoothing/bandwidth hyperparameters (unlike copula-based MGPs), which is a genuine practical advantage clearly demonstrated across the diverse experimental suite.
weaknesses: The central claim of validity rests entirely on empirical diagnostics rather than theory; while this is disclosed, it means the 'posterior' guarantee is essentially heuristic, and the paper's own a.c.i.d. diagnostic (Appendix C) is inconclusive (confounded with numerical precision issues at the scales tested), leaving genuine uncertainty about whether TabMGP posteriors are well-defined in the limit.

Scope is narrower than the framing suggests: despite motivating the work around general loss-defined functionals theta(F), all experiments use only linear/logistic/multinomial regression coefficients as the functional of interest -- more complex or nonlinear estimands are not explored, limiting evidence for the claimed generality.

The treatment of covariates X (Bayesian bootstrap sampling, discrete and non-smooth) versus Y|X (TabPFN) is somewhat ad hoc; the paper does not fully justify why this asymmetric treatment yields coherent joint uncertainty, especially since Bayesian bootstrap alone is noted elsewhere as unsuitable when smoothness of F_infinity matters.

Coverage results frequently show substantial over-coverage (many entries at 0.97-1.00 against a 0.95 target), which, while not inherently 'wrong,' suggests credible sets may often be conservative/loose rather than tightly calibrated, complicating the narrative that TabMGP is simultaneously well-calibrated and small.

The Copula baseline's bandwidth is fixed ad hoc at 0.8 rather than tuned via the original marginal-likelihood procedure (justified because that procedure 'produces values too small'), which could bias the baseline comparison in TabMGP's favor and reduces confidence in the head-to-head comparisons.

Computational cost is substantially higher than all baselines (70-200s per sample vs. near-instantaneous for BB/Asymptotic), and the real-data ground truth is itself only an empirical-distribution proxy rather than a true population target, both of which somewhat limit the strength of the frequentist coverage claims.

TabPFN's context-length limitation (10,000) constrains applicability to larger n regimes, and the paper's own diagnostics (Fig. 8) show a nontrivial fraction of low-diversity dataset realizations lead to unstable/diverging theta(F_N) trajectories, an edge-case failure mode acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.
